Villanova enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a 24-7 team that finished 15-5 in BIG EAST play, based on its March 7, 2026 regular-season finale against Xavier. Earlier checkpoints confirm the climb: Villanova was 15-5 and 6-3 in the league on January 24, 2026, then 22-6 and 13-4 on February 25 before closing 24-7, 15-5. The year-to-date statistical profile shows 77.2 points per game, 45.7 percent shooting from the floor, 35.3 percent from 3, and only 10.1 turnovers per game, which fits a controlled, half-court identity under first-year coach Kevin Willard. ([villanova.com](https://villanova.com/news/2026/3/7/mens-basketball-brennan-askew-star-on-senior-day-as-cats-down-xavier-91-78.aspx))

Offensively, this is a traditional Willard team in structure but not in tempo panic: multiple guards, deliberate spacing, and heavy reliance on ball-screen creation, drive-and-kick reads, and second-side 3-point shooting. The clearest evidence is in the assist and turnover numbers. Villanova averages 15.5 assists against 10.1 turnovers on the season, and in a key road overtime win at Xavier on February 17 it posted 24 assists with only six turnovers, after Willard said, "We're going to take a lot of 3's." That game also showed how Villanova uses bench spacing pieces to tilt matchups: Devin Askew hit three first-half 3-pointers, Malachi Palmer added another, and Bryce Lindsay buried the overtime tie-breaking 3 to snap an 83-83 game. In the December 19 overtime win over Wisconsin, Villanova opened OT with a designed action that produced a Bryce Lindsay 3, then hit another Lindsay triple on the next surge; that is a named example of Willard scripting overtime offense rather than simply freelancing. Against Marquette on January 10, Villanova hit its first six shots, including three Matt Hodge 3-pointers, another sign that the staff is comfortable using pick-and-pop or trail-pop forwards to stretch coverage early. ([villanova.com](https://villanova.com/news/2026/2/17/mens-basketball-wildcats-outlast-xavier-92-89-in-overtime.aspx?utm_source=openai))

The offensive engine is balance rather than one-volume scorer. ESPN’s season stats list Tyler Perkins at 13.7 points, 5.4 rebounds, and 36.6 percent from 3; Duke Brennan at 12.4 points and 10.3 rebounds on 65.7 percent shooting; Acaden Lewis at 12.3 points and 5.3 assists; Bryce Lindsay at 11.9 points with 72 made 3-pointers; Devin Askew at 10.0 points and 40.8 percent from deep; and Matt Hodge at 9.2 points with 50 made 3-pointers. That distribution explains the scheme: Lewis initiates, Brennan is the interior finisher and offensive-rebound target, Perkins is the wing scorer who can also rebound, Lindsay and Askew are floor-spacers, and Hodge is a stretch frontcourt piece. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/222/villanova-wildcats))

Defensively, Villanova has been more sound than spectacular, and its best possessions come when it can keep the game in the half court. The team allows 69.1 points per game through the 25-game Sports-Reference snapshot, and Willard’s own postgame comments repeatedly point to transition defense and physicality as swing factors. In the January 17 loss to St. John’s, he said the Red Storm had "continue[d] to put pressure on you in transition," and Villanova was outscored 42-22 in the paint. In the January 24 overtime loss at UConn, Willard said, "I thought we did some really good things defensively to keep them off balance," and the game was tied at 67 with 1:43 left in OT before UConn closed on an 8-0 run. In the February 14 win at Creighton, Willard specifically praised the first-half defensive effort as "really solid," and Villanova used a 16-3 first-half burst to take control. The pattern is clear: Villanova wants to wall off the lane, make teams score over the top in the half court, and avoid scramble possessions. When opponents impose size or downhill force, that scheme bends. Creighton’s January 7 win is the best example: the Bluejays shot 15-of-19 on 2-point tries in the second half and .667 overall after halftime. ([villanova.com](https://villanova.com/news/2026/1/17/mens-basketball-wildcats-drop-86-79-decision-to-st-john-s.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Willard’s in-game adjustment history this season is documented by several specific games. On January 3 at Butler, Villanova trailed 33-30 at halftime, then opened the second half on a 7-0 run and scored 55 second-half points in an 85-67 win; that is a textbook halftime adjustment game. On February 10 against Marquette, Villanova trailed 66-57 with 6:13 left and still won 77-74, with Perkins and Lewis making the decisive late plays. On February 17 at Xavier, Willard went to his bench after an early 11-0 Xavier spurt; the reserves changed the rhythm, and Villanova recovered to win 92-89 in overtime. On the other side, the January 7 Creighton loss revealed an adjustment miss: Villanova defended well for 20 minutes, but Creighton’s size and interior scoring flipped the game after halftime. ([villanova.com](https://villanova.com/news/2026/1/3/mens-basketball-55-point-secnd-half-carries-wildcats-pasat-butler-85-67.aspx))

Clutch and late-game execution is mostly a strength. Villanova beat Wisconsin 76-66 in overtime on December 19 after a 56-56 tie at the end of regulation, then outscored the Badgers 20-10 in OT. Villanova beat Marquette 76-73 on January 10, with Hodge and Perkins making key baskets in the final two minutes and Lewis assisting on Perkins’ bucket with 11 seconds left. Villanova beat Providence 88-82 on January 13, where Brennan made two clutch free throws after Providence cut the margin to five. Villanova lost a close one at UConn on January 24, 75-67 in overtime, after the game was tied at 67 with 1:43 to play in OT. Villanova beat Marquette again on February 10, rallying from nine down in the final 6:13. Villanova beat Xavier 92-89 in overtime on February 17, with Lindsay’s overtime 3 breaking an 83-83 tie. These are not generic “toughness” claims; they are repeated score-state examples of a team comfortable in one-possession games. ([villanova.com](https://villanova.com/news/2025/12/19/mens-basketball-overtime-surge-carries-cats-past-wisconsin-76-66.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Key players: Perkins is the lead scorer and late-clock wing option. He averages 13.7 points, and his standout moments include 23 points against St. John’s on January 17, 22 points against Marquette on February 10, 19 points versus Wisconsin on December 19, and 17 points with 11 rebounds at Creighton on February 14. Brennan is the interior anchor: 12.4 points, 10.3 rebounds, 65.7 percent shooting, 14 double-doubles by March 7, plus 21 points and 12 rebounds at Creighton, 16 points and 14 boards at UConn, and 20 points and 13 rebounds against Xavier on Senior Day. Lewis is the freshman shot-creator and best passer: 12.3 points and 5.3 assists for the season, 20 points and eight assists at Marquette on January 10, 20 points against Creighton on January 7, 21 points, seven rebounds, and six assists at Xavier on February 17, 26 points against Georgetown on February 7, and a season-high 12 assists against Xavier on March 7. Lindsay is the movement shooter: 11.9 points per game and the overtime dagger at Xavier, plus the back-to-back overtime 3s that broke Wisconsin. Askew is the sixth-man scorer, averaging 10.0 points overall and 15.2 points per game in BIG EAST play for Perkins? No—15.2 in league play belongs to Perkins; Askew was later named BIG EAST Sixth Man of the Year and averages 10.3 points across 19 games in that reserve role. Hodge adds frontcourt spacing, averaging 9.2 points and opening the January 10 Marquette game with three early 3-pointers. Palmer is a depth wing whose 10 bench points at Creighton on February 14 and 10 against Georgetown on February 7 show he can swing a tournament game in a short burst. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/222/villanova-wildcats))

Notable wins: Wisconsin, 76-66 in OT on December 19, showed composure and a capacity to execute set offense in extra time. Marquette, 76-73 on January 10, showed road poise and ball security through Lewis’s eight assists. Providence, 88-82 on January 13, showed they could withstand a late run. Creighton, 80-69 on February 14, was a statement revenge win after the earlier loss, powered by Brennan’s 21 and 12 and a game-defining 16-3 first-half burst. Xavier, 92-89 in OT on February 17, showed lineup flexibility and offensive resilience after an early hole. Georgetown, 80-73 on February 7, highlighted Lewis’s star upside with 26 points. The regular-season finale, 91-78 over Xavier on March 7, showed top-end offensive ceiling: 35-of-62 from the field, 13-of-31 from 3, and 24 assists. ([villanova.com](https://villanova.com/news/2025/12/19/mens-basketball-overtime-surge-carries-cats-past-wisconsin-76-66.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Notable losses: BYU beat Villanova 71-66 on November 3, an early neutral-floor indicator that this new roster could be sped up by physical, disciplined opponents. Michigan beat Villanova 89-61 on December 9, a 28-point loss that exposed how badly the Wildcats can look when the shot creation dries up. Creighton’s 76-72 win on January 7 revealed issues guarding size and interior finishing after halftime. St. John’s beat Villanova 86-79 on January 17 and then 89-57 on February 28/March 1 weekend, exposing problems against elite physical pressure and transition force. UConn beat Villanova twice, 75-67 in OT on January 24 and 73-63 on February 21, showing that Villanova can compete possession-for-possession with a top national seed but struggles to finish against top-end shot-making and size. ([s3.amazonaws.com](https://s3.amazonaws.com/sidearm.sites/bigeast.com/documents/2026/1/29/MBB_Stats_0129.pdf))

As for the head coach’s NCAA tournament history, Kevin Willard arrived at Villanova in 2025 after leading Maryland to the 2025 Sweet 16. St. John’s game notes state that before Villanova he coached Maryland for three years and previously coached Seton Hall. The user asked for rounds reached and years; from the currently gathered 2026-season sources, the directly documented tournament benchmark is Maryland reaching the 2025 Sweet 16. These same sources do not provide a complete year-by-year list of all Willard NCAA finishes, so the safest scouting conclusion is narrower: Villanova has a coach with documented recent second-weekend experience, specifically the 2025 Sweet 16 at Maryland, plus a long major-conference résumé at Seton Hall and Maryland. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/documents/download/2026/2/27/29_Villanova_2-28.pdf))

Bottom line: Villanova is a disciplined, guard-led, half-court tournament team with multiple shot-makers, a true rebounder/finisher in Brennan, and a freshman creator in Lewis who already has several high-leverage road performances. Its best version shares the ball, limits turnovers, and turns late games into execution contests. Its vulnerability is equally clear: teams with overwhelming physicality, transition pressure, or frontcourt size—like St. John’s, Creighton in the first meeting, and UConn—can drag the Wildcats out of their comfort zone.

Villanova enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament profile as a strong-but-not-elite national team whose résumé is better than its pure predictive metrics. The broadest consensus markers I could verify put the Wildcats in the back end of the protected-at-large tier rather than among the true title favorites. NCAA’s March 27 NET sheet lists Villanova at No. 35 nationally with a 24-8 record, including a 2-6 mark in Quad 1, 8-1 in Quad 2, 9-1 in Quad 3, and 5-0 in Quad 4. ESPN’s BPI page, last updated March 5, 2026, places Villanova 61st nationally. Sports-Reference lists Villanova at 24-7 in the regular season, 15-5 in the Big East, with an SRS of 17.13 and strength of schedule of 10.10, ranking 37th and 47th respectively. That combination tells a clear story: the résumé is tournament-caliber and solid, but computer models driven by possession-level dominance are less convinced than the win-loss column suggests.

At the raw team level, Villanova has been efficient offensively but not overwhelmingly so. Sports-Reference lists the Wildcats at 115.3 points scored per 100 possessions and 104.8 allowed per 100 possessions, good for offensive rating rank 72 and defensive rating rank 129 nationally. Using cumulative box-score totals from Villanova and ESPN team stat pages, Villanova has scored 2,469 points on 1,912 field-goal attempts, 598 free-throw attempts, 369 offensive rebounds, and 324 turnovers. That yields an estimated offensive efficiency of about 115.9 points per 100 possessions, consistent with the Sports-Reference figure. The same sources show 2,257 points allowed, which implies a defensive efficiency right around 110 points per 100 possessions by simple possession estimation. The practical takeaway is that this is an offense-first team with a clearly positive, but not dominant, efficiency margin.

Stylistically, Villanova is closer to modern perimeter-oriented Big East offense than to the old slow-grind Villanova stereotype. Estimated possessions come out to roughly 66.6 per game, a moderate tempo rather than a crawl. ESPN shows the Wildcats averaging 77.2 points, 34.5 rebounds, 15.5 assists, 10.1 turnovers, and shooting 45.7% from the field, 35.3% from three, and 69.4% from the line. From those cumulative totals, Villanova’s three-point attempt rate is approximately 45.7%, meaning nearly half of its shots come from beyond the arc. Free-throw rate is about 31.3 free-throw attempts per 100 field-goal attempts, which is adequate but not overwhelming. Turnover percentage, estimated from team totals, is about 13.0%, which is very good and one of the cleaner indicators of what Villanova does best: it gets shots up and does not waste possessions.

The four factors sketch the offense more clearly. Villanova’s estimated effective field-goal percentage, using ESPN’s totals of 415 made field goals and 308 made threes on 873 total field goals made and 1,912 attempts, comes out to about 51.9%. That is good, though not explosive. The turnover rate, as noted, is strong at roughly 13.0%. Offensive rebounding is decent but not a defining strength; Villanova collected 369 offensive boards and 734 defensive boards, while opponents had 377 offensive rebounds against Villanova. That points to an offense that mostly survives on shotmaking plus ball security, not on living at the rim or creating huge second-chance volume. Duke Brennan’s 10.3 rebounds per game and 4.0 offensive boards per game are central here; he is the interior counterweight that prevents the roster from becoming purely jump-shot dependent.

The shooting profile is a little more nuanced than the eye test. Conventional wisdom would probably label Villanova as a really good shooting team, and there is some truth to that: Devin Askew is at 40.8% from three, Tyler Perkins 36.6%, Matt Hodge 36.8%, and Bryce Lindsay has made 72 threes. But as a team they are at 35.3% from deep and just 45.7% overall from the floor, which is good rather than elite. The offense is better described as high-volume perimeter creation with low turnover drag than as an unstoppable shotmaking machine. In other words, they feel hotter than they numerically are because of attempt volume and lineup spacing.

The recent-form story is mixed, and this is where the profile becomes interesting. Villanova won eight of its final ten regular-season games, including wins over Marquette, Creighton, Xavier, Butler, DePaul, and another Xavier game, and it finished 15-5 in league play. But the closing stretch also included a 57-89 blowout loss at St. John’s and then a 64-78 loss to Georgetown on March 12. So the trend is not clean upward acceleration; it is more of a team that banked quality conference wins, stabilized after midseason, but still showed volatility against physical or defensively disruptive opponents. The low-turnover offense gives them a high baseline, yet the defense has not consistently held up against better opposition, which helps explain the gap between résumé metrics and predictive ones.

That divergence from the eye test is probably the single most important analytical point. A casual observer sees a 24-win Big East team under Kevin Willard, veteran guard play from Devin Askew, lead creation from Acaden Lewis, wing scoring from Tyler Perkins and Bryce Lindsay, and a legitimate rebounding anchor in Brennan. The numbers, however, say Villanova is not really built like a classic second-weekend favorite. NET at 35 and BPI at 61 indicate that the market of predictive systems views them as vulnerable. The résumé says “dangerous tournament team”; the possession data says “solid but beatable, especially if the threes flatten out or if opponents pressure them into a more interior, physical game.”

So the full statistical read is this: Villanova is a competent, balanced tournament entrant with a reliable offense, strong ball security, meaningful perimeter volume, and enough size via Brennan to avoid being one-dimensional. Its strength of schedule is respectable, and the Big East finish confirms the team is better than a bubble-level outfit. But the defense is only middling by national-tournament standards, the high-end wins are not abundant, and the predictive rankings are materially cooler than the résumé. That makes Villanova the sort of team that can absolutely win a first-round game and stress a better seed, but whose path to a deep run likely depends on shooting variance breaking in its favor and on avoiding opponents that can both switch its perimeter actions and punish its defense inside.

Villanova enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a good-but-beatable half-court offense built more on execution, spacing and shotmaking than overwhelming rim pressure. Sports-Reference lists the Wildcats at 77.6 points per game with a 24-7 record, while their team shooting splits are .456 overall and .350 from three. They average 15.1 assists against 9.4 turnovers, which points to a controlled offense rather than a chaotic, turnover-prone one. Their roster also confirms the structural profile: Devin Askew (6-5), Tyler Perkins (6-4), Bryce Lindsay (6-3) and Malachi Palmer (6-6) give them size on the perimeter, while Duke Brennan and the 7-foot centers Braden Pierce and Nico Onyekwere supply interior size, but not elite frontcourt burst across the board. Kevin Willard’s staff has clearly leaned into a methodical, matchup-reading style rather than pure tempo ball. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/villanova/?utm_source=openai))

**Style of play — and the specific tactics that disrupt it**
Villanova is most comfortable when it can run clean half-court offense through guards making simple reads into paint touches, kick-outs and secondary actions. The evidence is in their better wins: against Providence on January 13, 2026, Villanova scored 88 on the road and led 46-34 at half; against Providence again on January 30, they generated 10 first-half Friar turnovers and then finished on a 38-30 closing burst. In the January 17 loss to St. John’s, however, Villanova was knocked off rhythm by a game that included "¾ court and full court trapping," and St. John’s then used a 27-12 surge to open the second half. In the February 28 rematch, St. John’s was even more disruptive: Villanova was "hard-pressed to generate points against the physical brand of pressure," shot 7-of-27 in the first half, and trailed 48-23 at the break. The tactical lesson is clear: crowd handlers early, deny reversal passes, and turn their possession game into a scramble game. Their offense looks much less comfortable once initial spacing gets distorted and they are forced into late-clock creation. ([villanova.com](https://villanova.com/news/2026/1/13/mens-basketball-wildcats-hold-off-providence-88-82.aspx))

**Press and zone vulnerability**
There is direct evidence that both pressure and length-based zone can bother them. La Salle’s November 19, 2025 recap explicitly noted that "a 3-2 zone with length at every position had slowed Villanova" and forced late-clock offense. Villanova still won that game 70-55 because La Salle could not score enough, but the possession-level problem showed up. Against pressure, the St. John’s games are the best evidence. On January 17, the Red Storm mixed pace with 3/4-court and full-court trapping and then buried Villanova with a 27-12 opening stretch to the second half after two quick Villanova turnovers. On February 28, St. John’s forced steals that led directly to points, built a 16-0 edge in points off turnovers over the first 12:09, and had Villanova at 5-of-15 from the field in that span. UConn’s January 24 overtime win offers a third example: in OT, UConn forced a turnover, scored in transition to cut the lead to 64-63, then created another steal under a minute left that set up a drive and a four-point lead. If you want a blueprint, it is not passive zone; it is active zone or man-pressure with length, then immediate attack after live-ball turnovers. ([villanova.com](https://villanova.com/news/2025/11/19/mens-basketball-villanova-posts-a-70-55-big-five-win-at-la-salle.aspx?utm_source=openai))

**Preferred pace — and how to force the opposite**
Villanova can win fast games, but that is not its preferred environment. Their assist-turnover profile and half-court shot profile suggest control; their better offensive games typically come when they can get organized and play from advantage rather than from constant change of ends. Even Willard’s own comments frame this: before the St. John’s matchup he said, "They play at a fast pace, and you’ve got to match their pace," adding that on the road he ordinarily does not like to do that. In the Xavier overtime win on February 17, Willard again said, "The pace Xavier plays at it is really fast and that makes it tough." Villanova survived because all five starters scored in double figures, not because that game shape favored them. To force the opposite of Villanova’s comfort zone, speed them up after makes and misses: quick inbound pressure, early drag screens, rim runs at Brennan/Pierce, and hard attacks before their shell defense gets set. St. John’s did this on January 17, scoring 42 points in the paint and using transition pressure to break the game open. ([villanova.com](https://villanova.com/news/2026/2/17/mens-basketball-wildcats-outlast-xavier-92-89-in-overtime.aspx?utm_source=openai))

**Size and athleticism mismatches at each position**
At point/lead guard, Askew is a big guard at 6-5, but pressure guards with more burst can still tilt him into a containment role rather than an attacking role. St. John’s guards repeatedly got downhill in both losses, and Willard specifically referenced Dillon Mitchell changing their gear. At the 2/3 spots, Villanova has solid size with Perkins (6-4), Lindsay (6-3) and Palmer (6-6), but not elite top-end explosion; against more powerful slashers, that group can be driven backward. On the wing, Matt Hodge adds another bigger body, but the February 28 St. John’s game showed how vulnerable Villanova becomes when wing depth is compromised after Hodge’s injury. Up front, Brennan is productive and physical, but St. John’s still posted a 42-22 paint edge on January 17 and a 22-6 paint edge in the first half on February 28. Against true vertical athletes or fast second-jump bigs, Villanova’s centers offer size but not necessarily mobility. Braden Pierce is 7-0, 245 and Nico Onyekwere is 7-1, 240, which helps against brute size; it does not automatically solve space-defense issues. The practical mismatch hunt is this: put their bigs in repeated ball-screen coverage, then force the low man to rotate from shooters. ([villanova.com](https://villanova.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster))

**Isolation vs. team offense tendencies**
Without direct Synergy access, the most defensible reading from the available 2025-26 data is that Villanova leans team offense over isolation. Their 15.1 assists per game against 9.4 turnovers, plus game recaps highlighting ball movement and interior feeds, support that. In the January 13 Providence win, Villanova’s offense repeatedly created sharp interior feeds to Duke Brennan when Providence pressed out on shooters. In the January 17 St. John’s game, once pressure broke their rhythm, the offense became less efficient because they were dragged away from read-and-react basketball. So while exact isolation-play percentages are not publicly available in the sources I could verify, the available evidence supports a team-offense identity: assisted baskets, advantage passing, and secondary creation over high-volume pure isolation. That means the best defensive tactic is to switch selectively on the perimeter while staying home on shooters, forcing late-clock one-on-one creation from players who are more comfortable reading help than beating set defenders repeatedly. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/villanova/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

**Transition offense and defense frequency**
Again, full possession-type frequencies were not publicly available from a primary source I could verify, but the game evidence is strong enough to identify tendencies. Villanova can generate transition offense when defense fuels it: versus Providence, they built an 8-2 transition edge in the first half on January 13, and Malachi Palmer said, "We were just able to play defense and let our defense create offense for us." Against St. John’s and UConn, the other side of the coin showed up: St. John’s built transition pressure into a 42-22 paint advantage on January 17, then a 16-0 points-off-turnovers edge in the first 12:09 on February 28; UConn turned an overtime turnover into transition points and then created another steal in the closing minute. So Villanova is not a pure run-first team, but its transition offense spikes when live-ball defense creates it, and its transition defense becomes vulnerable when the game gets sped up by pressure turnovers. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/documents/download/2026/1/15/VUMBB_Game18Notes-StJohns.pdf))

**Coaching adaptability**
Willard’s staff does adjust in-game. The best direct example is from the January 13 Providence game notes cited in St. John’s materials: when Providence pressed shooters, Villanova responded by feeding Brennan inside, where he scored six points in the first 4:21 of the second half. The February 17 Xavier win also showed bench-rotation adaptation; Willard explicitly praised the bench for changing the game against Xavier’s pace. And in the January 24 UConn game, Villanova stayed competitive deep into regulation and overtime despite shooting only 20-of-59 (.339), which suggests a defensive game-plan adjustment rather than an offensive outlier. I would not describe the staff as radically experimental, but they are clearly willing to toggle lineups, use different entry points and attack where pressure leaves openings. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/documents/download/2026/1/15/VUMBB_Game18Notes-StJohns.pdf))

**Concrete gameplan — to beat this team you must…**
1. **Pick up full or 3/4 court after every dead ball.** St. John’s proved that sustained pressure can derail Villanova’s rhythm; the Red Storm used trapping pressure on January 17 and then produced a 16-0 points-off-turnovers edge early in the February 28 game. ([villanova.com](https://villanova.com/news/2026/1/17/mens-basketball-wildcats-drop-86-79-decision-to-st-john-s.aspx))
2. **Show length in zone on secondary possessions.** La Salle’s 3-2 zone with length slowed Villanova even in a game it lost. Use it as a changeup, especially after timeouts. ([villanova.com](https://villanova.com/news/2025/11/19/mens-basketball-villanova-posts-a-70-55-big-five-win-at-la-salle.aspx?utm_source=openai))
3. **Run at their frontcourt before it gets set.** St. John’s generated 42 paint points on January 17 and 22-6 paint points in the first half on February 28. Sprint drag screens at Brennan/Pierce and force backpedal coverage. ([villanova.com](https://villanova.com/news/2026/1/17/mens-basketball-wildcats-drop-86-79-decision-to-st-john-s.aspx))
4. **Do not over-help off shooters in the half court.** Villanova still has enough passing to punish obvious rotations; Providence got burned when it pressed too far out and Villanova hit Brennan on interior feeds. Stay attached, switch selectively, and make them finish over size. ([redstormsports.com](https://redstormsports.com/documents/download/2026/1/15/VUMBB_Game18Notes-StJohns.pdf))
5. **Win the live-ball turnover battle.** Villanova is excellent when its defense creates offense, as shown by the 10 first-half Providence turnovers on January 30 and the 8-2 transition edge on January 13. If you let them steal easy points, you feed the exact game script they want. ([villanova.com](https://villanova.com/news/2026/1/31/mens-basketball-askew-helps-propel-wildcats-past-providence-87-73.aspx))

Bottom line: Villanova is dangerous when the game is organized, the ball moves side-to-side, and Brennan plus the veteran guards can play through structure. To beat them, you must make the game ugly, fast, physical and lateral. Pressure the ball, mix in long zone looks, attack the paint in transition, and force their half-court decision-makers to become late-clock isolation scorers instead of advantage passers. ([villanova.com](https://villanova.com/news/2026/1/17/mens-basketball-wildcats-drop-86-79-decision-to-st-john-s.aspx))
